notes: Complete judgment on jurisdiction for creditors' schemes of arrangement involving Cayman and Jersey companies.

enrichment.short_title: English court has jurisdiction to convene meetings for cross-border creditors' schemes where Drax debt restructuring has sufficient English connection
key_facts: Drax Holdings Ltd (Cayman) and InPower Ltd (Jersey), part of the AES Drax Group owning Drax Power Station, proposed linked Schemes of Arrangement to restructure approximately £1 billion of debt after TXU Europe's collapse terminated the power purchase agreement.

Creditors included Senior Bondholders, Eurobond coupon holders, hedging banks and InPower's bank lenders; the Schemes would consolidate debt in a new Jersey company and provide new secured debt, cash and shares in a new holding company.
English law governed key financing documents; security included the Yorkshire power station and English company shares; Eurobond coupons were held in London.
Parallel scheme applications were made in Cayman, Jersey and England; meetings were to be held in London for all three jurisdictions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application under section 425(1) of the Companies Act 1985 for orders convening creditor meetings to consider Schemes of Arrangement; preliminary issue on jurisdiction for foreign companies.
enrichment.outcome: Court satisfied it has jurisdiction to order meetings and, if sanctioned, approve the Schemes; written reasons given for jurisdiction differing from the companies' original presentation.
enrichment.ratio: Foreign unregistered companies may be subject to section 425 schemes if they are companies liable to be wound up under the Insolvency Act 1986; the Latreefers three conditions (connection with England, benefit to applicants, jurisdiction over interested persons) go to discretion on winding up rather than jurisdiction under section 425, so they need not be satisfied for schemes; for creditors' schemes an English connection arises where English law governs obligations and English assets are secured, especially when parallel orders are made in countries of incorporation.
legal_issues: Whether the English court has jurisdiction under section 425 to summon meetings and sanction schemes for foreign companies
Whether the Latreefers preconditions for winding up foreign companies apply as jurisdictional requirements for section 425
Whether sufficient connection with England exists to exercise jurisdiction over creditors' schemes for Cayman and Jersey companies

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment on provocation and loss of self-control under section 3 Homicide Act.

enrichment.short_title: Murder conviction upheld where judge rightly refused to leave provocation because defendant denied loss of self-control
key_facts: Following conviction for murder and life sentence at Kingston Crown Court, the appellant appealed on the basis that the trial judge should have left provocation to the jury under section 3 of the Homicide Act 1957.

The appellant strangled Li Ming Shen in July 2001; medical evidence showed rigor mortis and strangulation injuries consistent with sustained pressure; the prosecution case was intentional killing after a violent relationship.

The defence case was lack of intent; the appellant claimed he put his hand on her throat without squeezing hard; provocation was invited by both counsel but the judge declined, finding minimal evidence of loss of self-control.
In evidence the appellant denied at any stage losing control because of the victim's behaviour.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave of the Single Judge; Crown Court murder trial before HHJ Tilling.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 3 of the Homicide Act 1957 the judge must decide whether there is evidence of provoking conduct resulting in loss of self-control; if, even on a view most favourable to the accused, there is insufficient material for a reasonable possibility of both elements, provocation must not be left; mere speculative possibility or minimal evidence is insufficient following R v Acott and R v Jones; where the defendant's own evidence denies loss of self-control, provocation need not be left despite potentially provoking conduct.
legal_issues: Whether the trial judge erred in refusing to leave provocation to the jury
What evidential threshold is required for section 3 Homicide Act provocation
Whether minimal evidence of loss of self-control suffices to require a provocation direction

notes: Full Beatson J judgment on MHRT conditional discharge and nature or degree misdirection.

enrichment.short_title: MHRT conditional discharge quashed where tribunal treated nature and degree of mental disorder as conjunctive rather than disjunctive
key_facts: DH was detained under a hospital order with restriction order after stabbing another patient while an in-patient in 1998; he had a history of schizophrenia, alcohol and drug misuse, self-harm and violence.

He had been conditionally discharged in 2001, recalled in January 2003 after alcohol and drug use and hostile behaviour, and the MHRT on 16 May 2003 ordered deferred conditional discharge to a staffed hostel with medication, supervision and drug screening conditions.
The Secretary of State applied to quash the Tribunal decision; DH opposed and argued the Tribunal decision was lawful.
Psychiatric evidence was divided: Dr Lyall supported continued detention; independent psychiatrist Dr Azuonye recommended absolute discharge.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Mental Health Review Tribunal decision ordering deferred conditional discharge under section 73(7); permission granted with stay and anonymity.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded on misdirection ground; Tribunal decision quashed and remitted to a differently constituted tribunal; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Section 72(1)(b) requires separate satisfaction of the appropriateness test (nature or degree of disorder) and the necessity test; treating nature and degree as conjunctive so that current low degree negates appropriateness is a misdirection; the Tribunal's finding that illness was of a nature to justify detention but not at present of a degree was inconsistent with answering the first statutory question; recall mechanisms cannot substitute for proper assessment of risk before discharge criteria are satisfied; proportionality under R (H) applies where uncertainty exists but does not excuse misapplication of statutory tests.
legal_issues: Whether the Tribunal misdirected itself by treating nature or degree as conjunctive
Whether risk when intoxicated must be considered in the appropriateness and necessity tests
Whether reliance on recall powers was a lawful substitute for addressing detention criteria
Whether Tribunal reasons were inadequate for rejecting expert evidence

notes: Complete Sullivan J judgment rejecting nine grounds of challenge to planning inspector's decision.

enrichment.short_title: Planning challenge fails over Abbeydale Court change of use to acute psychiatric beds; inspector's fear and apprehension analysis upheld

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Use Classes) Order 1987

key_facts: Inspector granted planning permission for change of use of the first floor of Abbeydale Court, Walthamstow, from a 34-bed elderly care unit to 22 acute psychiatric beds, increasing total acute beds from 13 to 35 alongside 11 intensive psychiatric beds.

Local residents and Waltham Forest Council objected on fear and apprehension, noise, amenity space, highway safety and sustainability grounds; the Council's refusal reason relied on over-intensive psychiatric use in a residential area contrary to policy ENV1.
Past incidents included a patient climbing onto the roof twice in August 2002; 630 patients had been admitted without public harm from attacks or nuisance.
The inspector relied on National Care Standards Commission regulation rather than fixed exclusion criteria for future admissions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 Town and Country Planning Act 1990 challenge to inspector's decision letter dated 1 May 2003 allowing planning appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Challenge rejected on all nine grounds; application dismissed; claimant ordered to pay Secretary of State's costs summarily assessed at £6,435.
enrichment.ratio: Fear and apprehension of local residents is a material planning consideration even if unjustified (Newport Borough Council); an inspector may place weight on statutory regulatory regimes (NCSC) operating effectively rather than freezing clinical admission policies in planning conditions; policy GCS1 applies to Class C2 uses including acute psychiatric units in residential areas; refusal to impose floor-specific bed conditions is lawful where condition 5 caps total beds by care type; planning permission does not require guarantee that harm will never occur.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector misapplied development plan policies GCS1 and ENV1
Whether reliance on NCSC regulation rather than exclusion criteria was an error of law
Whether past roof-climbing incidents were adequately weighed
Whether condition 5 unlawfully permitted development wider than the application
Whether outdoor amenity space and crime statistics were properly considered

notes: Complete Silber J judgment quashing clearly unfounded certificate on Article 3 suicide risk.

enrichment.short_title: Clearly unfounded human rights certificate quashed where Kosovo trauma victim's suicide risk on removal to Germany was arguable under Article 3
key_facts: Mr and Mrs K, Serbian Kosovans, sought asylum in the UK in 2000; Germany accepted return under the Dublin Convention Article 5.4.

Mrs K suffered severe PTSD and postpartum depression from war trauma including witnessing her father's killing and her nephew's murder; her son's resemblance to the murdered nephew triggered daily flashbacks.
She attempted suicide by drinking bleach when told she had to leave the UK; Dr Saddik's October 2003 report stated high suicide risk if removal to Germany was notified or implemented.
The Secretary of State certified the human rights claim as clearly unfounded on 2 and 17 October 2003 despite the medical evidence, proposing escorts and German reception arrangements.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review challenging Secretary of State certificates under section 93(2)(b) that return to Germany would not breach human rights; focus on 17 October 2003 decision after Dr Saddik's report.
enrichment.outcome: Certificate quashed on Article 3 ground; Secretary of State not entitled to maintain clearly unfounded certification; Article 8 claim not decided given Article 3 success.
enrichment.ratio: A claim is clearly unfounded only if after careful consideration the Secretary of State is reasonably satisfied it must clearly fail (Yogathas); if it is arguable on uncontradicted evidence that removal creates a real risk of significantly increased suicide risk, an Article 3 claim cannot be certified as clearly unfounded (Soumahoro in Razgar); proposed removal safeguards do not address suicide risk when notified in the UK before handover; N v Secretary of State concerns lack of medical resources abroad and does not displace Soumahoro on subjective trauma and suicide in the removing state.
legal_issues: Whether the Secretary of State could certify the human rights claim as clearly unfounded under section 93(2)(b)
Whether Article 3 is engaged by suicide risk from threatened removal to Germany under the Dublin Convention
Whether Soumahoro or N represents the governing law on medical/trauma Article 3 claims
Whether proposed escort and reception safeguards negate the Article 3 claim

notes: Complete Goldring J judgment on food business proprietor definition for corporate group.

enrichment.short_title: Greene King Plc held food business proprietor of Moorhen pub despite operating subsidiary owning premises and employing staff
key_facts: Environmental health officers found hygiene breaches at the Moorhen pub in Epping in July 2001: fly infestation, poor cleanliness, overflowing refuse and improper raw material storage.

Greene King Plc, a listed holding company with no employees, was prosecuted; Greene King Brewing and Retailing Ltd owned the premises, employed staff via service companies and conducted day-to-day trading.

A business sale agreement in 1997 transferred the operating business and Moorhen freehold to Retailing; confusion existed among staff and regulators as to which group company was the food business proprietor.
The Crown Court found the parent company's governance, budgeting, internal audit and health and safety oversight went beyond a mere shareholder role.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Crown Court dismissal of appeal from Epping Magistrates' convictions for Regulation 4 breaches; preliminary issue on correct defendant.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; question answered in the affirmative that Greene King Plc was a food business proprietor within section 53(1) of the Food Safety Act 1990.
enrichment.ratio: Proprietor under section 53(1) means the person by whom the business is carried on, not necessarily the owner or day-to-day operator (Ahmed v Nicholls); more than one corporate entity may be proprietor where group structure divides ownership, employment and management; carrying on a food business is not limited to physical food handling and may include entrepreneurial control, governance and monitoring; Salomon principles apply but a parent exceeding shareholder role may be criminally liable; criminal food safety legislation should be construed flexibly to protect consumers.
legal_issues: Whether Greene King Plc was the proprietor of a food business for Regulation 4 offences
Whether a holding company can be criminally liable when a subsidiary operates the premises
Whether multiple corporate entities may simultaneously be proprietors of one food business
Whether corporate confusion as to identity of proprietor determines criminal liability

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment on section 31(7) clean break and extension of term.

enrichment.short_title: Extension of periodical payments refused where judge failed to apply clean break duty under section 31(7) after fixed-term consent order
key_facts: Both parties were dental surgeons who divorced in 1997 after 17 years of marriage; a December 1998 consent order provided £1,000 per month periodical payments until 30 November 2002 without section 28(1)(a) bar on extension.

The wife applied in July 2002 to extend the term; she had a disabling condition limiting earning capacity, cohabited with a partner for over five years, and Judge Taylor extended payments at £500 per month on a joint lives basis.

The judge found the wife had part-time earning capacity of £15,000–£20,000 and her cohabitee could earn £20,000–£25,000; their combined income met expenses without drawing on savings after the original order ended.
The husband had a legitimate expectation that his obligations would end on the fixed date in the consent order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against HHJ Michael Taylor's order extending periodical payments under section 31 Matrimonial Causes Act 1973; permission granted on paper.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; wife's application for extension dismissed; no order for repayment of interim payments totalling about £6,000.
enrichment.ratio: On variation under section 31 the court must consider whether termination of financial obligations is appropriate without undue hardship (section 31(7)(a)); where a consent order fixed a termination date the payer's legitimate expectation and enhanced clean break duty require exceptional justification to extend; findings that combined household income sufficed without hardship cannot support a conclusion of substantial financial hardship; cohabitation is not equivalent to remarriage but long stable cohabitation may be weighed in the discretionary balance (Atkinson v Atkinson).
legal_issues: Whether the judge erred in extending periodical payments beyond the consent order termination date
Application of section 31(7)(a) clean break duty on variation after fixed-term order
Whether the wife's disability and cohabitation justified extension
Whether the judge's hardship finding was supported by his own factual findings on income

enrichment.short_title: SEN Tribunal decision set aside where ceasing statement wrongly treated School Action Plus provision as within mainstream school resources

statutes_considered.title: Special Educational Needs Code of Practice

key_facts: S, an 11-year-old dyslexic pupil, had a Statement of Special Educational Needs from January 2001 with LEA-provided specialist tuition; Blaenau Gwent LEA decided in January 2003 to cease maintaining the statement on transfer to comprehensive school.
The LEA proposed continuing comparable support from central Specific Learning Difficulties and Educational Psychology services under School Action Plus.
The Tribunal upheld cessation, finding needs could be met within mainstream school resources including central services.
The Code asks whether needs can be met within resources of the mainstream school, not merely within the graduated response framework.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 326 Education Act 1996 against Special Educational Needs Tribunal decision dated 30 July 2003 upholding cessation of statement.
enrichment.outcome: Tribunal decision set aside; matter remitted for rehearing; LEA ordered to pay appellant's costs including publicly funded assessment.
enrichment.ratio: When ceasing to maintain a statement the LEA and Tribunal must have regard to Code paragraphs 8:117–8:119; the question is whether special educational provision can be met within resources normally available to mainstream schools, not whether needs can be met at School Action Plus with external LEA services; specialist central services are not within school resources even if routinely delivered locally; the Tribunal must always consider whether progress would halt or reverse if statement provision ceased; failure to understand the Code is as defective as failing to have regard to it (Gransden).
legal_issues: Whether the Tribunal properly applied the SEN Code of Practice on ceasing to maintain a statement
Whether LEA central specialist services count as mainstream school resources
Whether the Tribunal considered whether progress would be halted without statement provision
Whether objectives in the statement had been achieved

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment on undue influence and educational trust gift.

enrichment.short_title: Niece ordered to repay £171,694 educational trust gift to aunt's estate after presumption of undue influence not rebutted
key_facts: Enid Davidge, a spinster, made gifts totalling £171,694 in 1995 to insurance policy trusts for her niece Penelope Cairns' daughters' school fees, selling shares and incurring about £30,000 capital gains tax.

Penelope held an Enduring Power of Attorney; Enid had strokes and declining health; John Cairns wrote misleading letters suggesting Enid could revoke or benefit from discretionary trusts she could not control.
Enid told her sister Margaret she had been made to sign everything; she had paid school fees from 1993 but the judge found the gift was not made after full, free and informed thought.
Penelope also misused the power of attorney for other transactions; Enid left half residuary estate to Penelope and half to Margaret's children in the US.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against HHJ Rich's order requiring Penelope Cairns to pay £171,694 equitable compensation to Enid's estate with interest; related orders on EPA account and substitution as executrix.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; personal compensation order upheld; leave to appeal to House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Under Royal Bank of Scotland v Etridge, trust and confidence plus a transaction calling for explanation shifts the evidential burden to the donee to show no undue influence; mistake as to trust terms and tax consequences does not necessarily rebut the presumption if the donor would not have gifted without the mistake; failure to ensure independent advice appropriate to the donor's needs prevents rebuttal; conduct need not be improper for undue influence to be established once the presumption is not displaced (Hammond v Osborne).
legal_issues: Whether Enid's £171,694 gift to educational trusts was procured by undue influence
Whether the evidential presumption of undue influence was rebutted
Whether mistake as to trust structure and tax freed the donor from presumed influence
Whether personal compensation was appropriate rather than setting aside the settlements

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment on consecutive section 80 longer than commensurate sentences.

enrichment.short_title: Twelve-year total sentence upheld for consecutive section 80(2)(b) terms on serial night-time indecent assaults
key_facts: Jonathan Backwell pleaded guilty to seven counts of indecent assault on women stalked late at night in Torquay over 18 months from August 2000.
He prowled in his car, followed victims on foot, attacked from behind groping breasts and vaginas; offences escalated to near-attempted rape on Faye Banks in September 2001.
He had a 1991 conviction for aggravated burglary and indecent assault with seven years imprisonment for similar predatory attacks.
Judge Cottle imposed six years per count as longer than commensurate sentences under section 80(2)(b); six counts concurrent, final count consecutive totalling 12 years.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against sentence by leave of the Single Judge; guilty pleas on morning of intended trial at Exeter Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; 12-year total sentence neither wrong in principle nor manifestly excessive.
enrichment.ratio: There is no principle forbidding consecutive sentences that in aggregate exceed the statutory maximum for a single offence; section 80 permitted maximum applies to each individual sentence, not the aggregate; consecutive longer than commensurate sentences may be imposed where each term does not exceed the individual maximum (R v Baker); Everleigh concerns consecutive longer-than-normal sentences on the same occasion, not consecutive section 80(2)(b) terms for separate offences; totality and public protection must be balanced.
legal_issues: Whether consecutive section 80(2)(b) sentences may exceed the statutory maximum in aggregate
Whether longer than commensurate sentences may run consecutively to each other
Whether 12 years total was manifestly excessive given guilty pleas and gap since previous conviction
